title: The subfields K_J of the fraction field of k[[x]][y] cut out by a p-basis
statement: Let $p$ be a prime number, $k$ a field of characteristic $p$ and $(t_i)_{i\in I}$ a $p$-basis of $k$: the monomials $t^E=\prod_it_i^{e_i}$ ($0\le e_i<p$, almost all $e_i=0$) form a basis of $k$ over its subfield $k^p=\{a^p:a\in k\}$. Let $n,m\ge0$ and $A=k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]][y_1,\ldots,y_m]$, the polynomial ring [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] in $y_1,\ldots,y_m$ over the formal power series ring $k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]; it is an integral domain, and let $K$ be its fraction field [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], $K^p=\{a^p:a\in K\}$. For a finite subset $J\subseteq I$ let $k_J\subseteq k$ be the subfield generated by $k^p$ and the $t_i$ with $i\in I\setminus J$, let $A_J=k_J[[x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p]][y_1^p,\ldots,y_m^p]\subseteq A$ be the subring of polynomials in $y_1^p,\ldots,y_m^p$ whose coefficients are power series $\sum_Ea_Ex_1^{pe_1}\cdots x_n^{pe_n}$ with all $a_E\in k_J$, and let $K_J\subseteq K$ be the fraction field of $A_J$ (the set of quotients $a/b$, $a,b\in A_J$, $b\ne0$). Then: (1) for every finite $J\subseteq I$, $A$ is a finitely generated $A_J$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]; (2) $K^p\subseteq K_J$ for every finite $J$; (3) $K^p=\bigcap_JK_J$, the intersection over all finite subsets $J\subseteq I$; (4) for finite $J,J'\subseteq I$ we have $K_{J\cup J'}\subseteq K_J\cap K_{J'}$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07P5 (lemma-power-series-ring-subfields, line 11521) and its proof; properties (2)-(4) are conditions (1)-(3) of Lemma Tag 07P4 (lemma-intersection-subfields), written out; tags verified in stacks-project/tags/tags

proof.text: ($A$ is a domain; the fields $K_J$.) The field $k$ is an integral domain, so $k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series] is an integral domain by [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-domain] (with $d=n$), and $A$, the polynomial ring [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] in $y_1,\ldots,y_m$ over it, is an integral domain by [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-domain]. Hence $(0)$ is a prime of $A$, its fraction field $K=A_{(0)}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a field, and $A\to K$, $a\mapsto a/1$, is injective; we regard $A\subseteq K$. For a subring $A'\subseteq A$ the set $\{a/b:a,b\in A',b\ne0\}$ contains $0,1$ and is closed under sums ($a/b+c/d=(ad+bc)/bd$, $bd\ne0$ as $A$ is a domain), products, negatives and inverses of nonzero elements ($(a/b)^{-1}=b/a$); so $K_J$ is a subfield of $K$ containing $A_J$, once $A_J$ is known to be a subring (Step 2).

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07P5 (lemma-power-series-ring-subfields, line 11521), proof (the statement takes K, the fraction field of the domain A, for granted; written out)

proof.text: (Coefficients; $A_J$ is a subring.) By [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] and [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series] an element $h\in A$ is $h=\sum_{g}H_gy^g$ with $H_g=\sum_ac_{a,g}x^a\in k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]$, $H_g=0$ for $g\in\mathbf N^m$ outside a finite set; so $h$ is given by its coefficients $c_{a,g}=c_{a,g}(h)\in k$, $(a,g)\in\mathbf N^n\times\mathbf N^m$, with $c_{\cdot,g}=0$ for almost all $g$, and conversely every such family is an element of $A$. Addition is coefficientwise and the product is $c_{a,g}(hh')=\sum c_{a',g'}(h)c_{a'',g''}(h')$, the finite sum over $(a',g')+(a'',g'')=(a,g)$. In particular multiplying by a monomial $x^ey^{g_0}$ shifts: $c_{a,g}(x^ey^{g_0}h)=c_{a-e,g-g_0}(h)$ if $a\ge e$, $g\ge g_0$ componentwise, and $0$ otherwise. Write $p\mathbf N^n=\{pq:q\in\mathbf N^n\}$. By its definition in the statement, $A_J$ is the set of $h\in A$ with $c_{a,g}(h)\in k_J$ for all $(a,g)$ and $c_{a,g}(h)=0$ unless $a\in p\mathbf N^n$ and $g\in p\mathbf N^m$. It contains $1$, is closed under sums and negatives, and under products: in the product formula a term $c_{a',g'}(h)c_{a'',g''}(h')$ with $h,h'\in A_J$ is nonzero only if $a',a''\in p\mathbf N^n$ and $g',g''\in p\mathbf N^m$, which forces $a\in p\mathbf N^n$, $g\in p\mathbf N^m$, and it lies in the subfield $k_J$. So $A_J$ is a subring of $A$.

proof.text: (A basis of $A$ over $A_J$; proof of (1).) Fix a finite $J$ and let $\mathcal B_J=\mathcal M_J\times\{0,\ldots,p-1\}^n\times\{0,\ldots,p-1\}^m$, a finite set with $p^{|J|+n+m}$ elements, and $b_{E,e,g}=t^Ex^ey^g\in A$. Claim: $(b_\beta)_{\beta\in\mathcal B_J}$ is a basis of the $A_J$-module $A$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Every $(a,g)\in\mathbf N^n\times\mathbf N^m$ is uniquely $(pq+e,pr+g_0)$ with $q\in\mathbf N^n$, $r\in\mathbf N^m$, $0\le e_i<p$, $0\le(g_0)_j<p$ (division with remainder in each component). Existence: let $h\in A$ and write each coefficient $c_{a,g}(h)=\sum_{E\in\mathcal M_J}c_{a,g,E}t^E$ with unique $c_{a,g,E}\in k_J$ (Step 3(b)); by uniqueness $c_{a,g,E}=0$ whenever $c_{a,g}(h)=0$. For $(E,e,g_0)\in\mathcal B_J$ let $\alpha_{E,e,g_0}$ be the element with coefficient $c_{pq+e,pr+g_0,E}\in k_J$ at $(pq,pr)$ and $0$ at exponents outside $p\mathbf N^n\times p\mathbf N^m$; it lies in $A$ (only the finitely many $r$ with $pr+g_0$ a $y$-exponent of $h$ give nonzero columns), hence in $A_J$ (Step 2). By the shift rule of Step 2, the coefficient of $\alpha_{E,e',g'}t^Ex^{e'}y^{g'}$ at $(pq+e,pr+g_0)$ is $t^E$ times the coefficient of $\alpha_{E,e',g'}$ at $(p q+e-e',pr+g_0-g')$, which is $0$ unless $e-e'\in p\mathbf Z^n$ and $g_0-g'\in p\mathbf Z^m$, i.e. $e'=e$, $g'=g_0$ (all entries in $[0,p)$). Hence $\sum_{\beta\in\mathcal B_J}\alpha_\beta b_\beta$ (a finite sum) has coefficient $\sum_Ec_{pq+e,pr+g_0,E}t^E=c_{pq+e,pr+g_0}(h)$ at every $(pq+e,pr+g_0)$, so it equals $h$. Uniqueness: if $\sum_\beta\alpha_\beta b_\beta=0$ with all $\alpha_\beta\in A_J$, the same computation gives at $(pq+e,pr+g_0)$: $\sum_{E\in\mathcal M_J}c_{pq,pr}(\alpha_{E,e,g_0})t^E=0$ with coefficients in $k_J$, so $c_{pq,pr}(\alpha_{E,e,g_0})=0$ by Step 3(b); as $\alpha_{E,e,g_0}$ has no other nonzero coefficients, $\alpha_\beta=0$ for all $\beta$. So $A$ is a free $A_J$-module with the finite basis $(b_\beta)$, in particular a finitely generated $A_J$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]: this is (1).

This implies that A_J -> A is finite'); finiteness proved here by an explicit basis instead of Algebra Lemma Tag 0394 (lemma-finite-after-completion)

proof.text: ($p$th powers in $A$; proof of (2).) Let $h=\sum_gH_gy^g\in A$ as in Step 2. In the ring $A$ of characteristic $p$, $(u+v)^p=u^p+v^p$, so by induction on the number of terms $h^p=\sum_gH_g^py^{pg}$ (a finite sum). By [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-frobenius-coefficientwise] (for the field $k$ of characteristic $p$), $H_g^p=\sum_ac_{a,g}^px^{pa}$. Hence: (a) $c_{pa,pg}(h^p)=c_{a,g}(h)^p$ and $c_{a',g'}(h^p)=0$ unless $a'\in p\mathbf N^n$, $g'\in p\mathbf N^m$. (b) Conversely, if $f\in A$ has $c_{a',g'}(f)=0$ unless $(a',g')\in p\mathbf N^n\times p\mathbf N^m$, and $c_{pa,pg}(f)=d_{a,g}^p$ with $d_{a,g}\in k$, then $f=h^p$ for the element $h\in A$ with coefficients $c_{a,g}(h)=d_{a,g}$ (it lies in $A$: $d_{\cdot,g}=0$ whenever $c_{\cdot,pg}(f)=0$, as $F$ is injective). Proof of (2): let $z=a/b\in K$, $a,b\in A$, $b\ne0$. By (a) the coefficients of $a^p$ and $b^p$ lie in $k^p\subseteq k_J$ (Step 3(c)) and vanish off $p\mathbf N^n\times p\mathbf N^m$, so $a^p,b^p\in A_J$ (Step 2), and $b^p\ne0$ as $A$ is a domain (Step 1). So $z^p=a^p/b^p\in K_J$: $K^p\subseteq K_J$ for every finite $J$.

proof.text: ($A\cap K_J=A_J$.) Fix $J$ and the basis $(b_\beta)_{\beta\in\mathcal B_J}$ of Step 4. It is linearly independent over $K_J$ in $K$: if $\sum_\beta\gamma_\beta b_\beta=0$ with $\gamma_\beta=u_\beta/v_\beta\in K_J$ ($u_\beta,v_\beta\in A_J$, $v_\beta\ne0$), put $v=\prod_\beta v_\beta\in A_J\setminus\{0\}$ (Step 1: $A$ is a domain); then $v\gamma_\beta\in A_J$ and $\sum_\beta(v\gamma_\beta)b_\beta=0$ in $A\subseteq K$, so all $v\gamma_\beta=0$ by the uniqueness in Step 4, and all $\gamma_\beta=0$. Now let $h\in A\cap K_J$. By Step 4, $h=\sum_\beta\alpha_\beta b_\beta$ with $\alpha_\beta\in A_J\subseteq K_J$. The element $\beta_0=(0,0,0)$ has $b_{\beta_0}=1$, so $(\alpha_{\beta_0}-h)b_{\beta_0}+\sum_{\beta\ne\beta_0}\alpha_\beta b_\beta=0$ is a relation with coefficients in $K_J$; by independence $h=\alpha_{\beta_0}\in A_J$. Hence $A\cap K_J=A_J$ (the inclusion $A_J\subseteq A\cap K_J$ is clear).

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07P5 (lemma-power-series-ring-subfields, line 11521), proof, second paragraph, 'Proof of (2) ... Since f/g^p in K_J we can write f/g^p = a/b^p with a in A_J ... Hence b^p f in A_J ... we conclude ... f in A_J': the source deduces f in A_J with the derivations d/dx_i, d/dy_j and k_J-derivations of k; here it is deduced from the basis of Step 4

proof.text: (Proof of (3).) By (2), $K^p\subseteq\bigcap_JK_J$. Conversely let $z\in\bigcap_JK_J$ and write $z=a/b$ with $a,b\in A$, $b\ne0$; put $f=ab^{p-1}\in A$, so that $z=f/b^p$. For every finite $J$: $b^p\in A_J\subseteq K_J$ (Step 5), so $f=zb^p\in K_J\cap A=A_J$ (Step 6). Thus, for every finite $J$, all coefficients of $f$ lie in $k_J$ and vanish off $p\mathbf N^n\times p\mathbf N^m$ (Step 2). So the coefficients of $f$ lie in $\bigcap_Jk_J=k^p$ (Step 3(c)): $c_{pa,pg}(f)=d_{a,g}^p$ with $d_{a,g}\in k$. By Step 5(b), $f=h^p$ with $h\in A$, and $z=h^p/b^p=(h/b)^p\in K^p$. Hence $K^p=\bigcap_JK_J$.

Since it is clear that A^p = cap_J A_J ... we conclude f in A^p as desired' (the clear equality written out with Steps 3(c) and 5(b))

proof.text: (Proof of (4).) Let $J,J'\subseteq I$ be finite. By Step 3(d), $k_{J\cup J'}\subseteq k_J\cap k_{J'}$, so by the description of Step 2 $A_{J\cup J'}\subseteq A_J\cap A_{J'}$, and every quotient $a/b$ with $a,b\in A_{J\cup J'}$ lies in $K_J\cap K_{J'}$: $K_{J\cup J'}\subseteq K_J\cap K_{J'}$.
